findings.statement: per-segment blooms recover only part of the fan tax at sixteen segments
findings.detail: bloom16 keeps 88.1% of k1, between fan16's 54.8% and oracle16's 185.8% (vs fan bloom16 vs fan16: greater 1.608x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 11.5%/4.6%); vs oracle bloom16 vs oracle16: less 0.474x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 11.5%/6.2%)). A fixed probe order pays ~8.5 filter queries per lookup before its first data probe, which is why a per-segment filter cannot reach the ceiling at this k

findings.statement: a global key->segment map recovers at least 95% of perfect routing
findings.detail: route16 at 204ns/read against oracle16's 125 (route16 vs oracle16: less 0.610x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 15.3%/6.2%)), 61.0% of the ceiling and 113.4% of k1. One hash lookup buys what sixteen filters cannot; the price is the one concession to global mutable state the next engine makes, and this is the number that justifies it

findings.statement: min/max fences prune nothing when segment key-ranges overlap
findings.detail: fence16 455ns/read against fan16 423 (fence16 vs fan16: NO DIFFERENCE (ratio 0.929, p=0.2101) -- within noise, not a result). Round-robin dealing makes every segment's range cover every key, so the fence admits every probe; recorded so the design never assumes fences route without key-partitioned sealing

notes: six arms interleaved in one process over two builds (one store, k segments, keys dealt round-robin so segment key-ranges fully overlap). fence16 consults per-segment min/max before probing; bloom16 a per-segment blocked Bloom (~10 bits/key, one 64-byte block per query); route16 a global key->segment hash map built at open; k1/fan16/oracle16 are f38's arms re-run so every comparison is same-run
predictions registered in filter-plan.md before the first full run
